title: Priors
text:
Uninformative priors
This is a complicated and often argued about question in Bayesian probability. If you have no knowledge of what the parameter is, then the argument is that you want the prior to be uninformative. But what does it mean for a prior to be uninformative?
A simple and often used choice for “uninformative” prior is a uniform prior. The uniform prior is not neccesarily a probability distribution. Yet even the uniform prior may not be “uninformative”.
Consider a simple example of observing \(5\) heads out of \(8\) coin tosses. We do not know if the coin is biased and we want to determine the probability of observing a head. The model that we would use to describe this situation is, \[
D \sim \text{Binomial}(10,p),
\] where \(D = 5\) and \(p\) is the unknown probability of observing a head.

title: Monte Carlo Methods
text:
Monte Carlo methods are a broad range of techniques associated with approximating solutions to mathematical problems through repeated sampling (hence the name after the famous casino). It is often likened to throwing darts at a problem and seeing which ones manage to stick.
To exemplify the a Monte Carlo approach, lets consider approximating the area of a circle with unit diameter.

As a first step, lets pretend that this is actually a really tough problem and we do not know the answer is \(\pi\).
For the second step, if the circle has unit diameter then we can place the circle entirely within a square with unit side lengths.
Next, lets throw 100 darts at our square!


dart_throw_locations = tibble::tibble(x = runif(100), y = runif(100))

The above code emulates the \(x\) and \(y\) location of each dart throw on our unit square. By visualising these plots over our circle, we can observe that some of the darts have succeeded in being inside the circle and some have not. We know that those darts had equal probability of being anywhere inside that square. Therefore, if we were to count the number of darts that were inside of the circle and compare that to the number that were outside of the circle, we are approximating the percentage area of the square that the circle takes up. Due to the fact that the square has an area of 1 unit\(^2\) we are approximating exactly the area of the circle (and not some scalar multiple of the circle).

title: Maximum Likelihood
text:
The maximum likelihood method for fitting mathematical models to data is perhaps the most common method used to fit models to data. In this approach, we must be able to write down our distributional assumptions for how the model fits the data. This is called the likelihood, \(\mathcal{L}\).
Assume we have a mathematical model with unknown parameters \(\theta\) and that we have collected \(N\) data points \(D\). The likelihood is expressed as, \[
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = p(D|\theta),
\] where \(p(D|\theta)\) is the probability of obtaining the observed data given known model parameters. By writing down the likelihood we are now in a position to decide on the value of \(\theta\) using strong theoretical foundations.
A reasonable argument to be made is that the value of \(\theta\) is that which maximises the probability of the data that we observed. As such, the model fit is obtained by solving \[
\hat{\theta} = \arg \max_{\theta \in \Theta} \mathcal{L}(\theta),
\] where \(\hat{\theta}\) is the fitted model parameters and \(\Theta\) is the entire parameter space. This is the maximum likelihood method.
In the examples provided we derived an exact form for the maximum likelihood estimate of our parameters. It is not always the case that we can obtain the maximum of our likelihood function using pen and paper. Therefore, we often use numerical techniques to approximate our solution.

title: Maximum Likelihood
section: Numerical methods for maximum likelihood problems.
text:
Numerical methods for maximum likelihood problems.
To obtain a numerical solution to a maximum likelihood problem you must look at the solution methods that maximise functions (of course right). There are a lot of different techniques and I will not go through them all, especially when the best approach is often problem dependent. A short list of techniques that find maximums (or equivalently minimums) are:

Newton-Rhapson
Nelder-Mead
Literally run every possible combination of parameters and check which is the largest or smallest (only suitable for finite parameter spaces but I have done this more often than you expect).

title: Bayesian Inference
text:
Bayesian inference is an alternative to inferring model fits from data. With maximum likelihood we have worked off the assumption that there is a true known value for the parameters and that the data varies. That is, we are interested with \(p(D|\theta\)). In direct contrast, for Bayesian inference we have that the data is known and we are interested in the probability distribution of the parameters, \(p(\theta|D)\). This is a subtle yet important point that has led to constant confusion and arguments. The two points of view are also related through Bayes’ Theorem.






NoneBayes’ Theorem



\[
p(A|B) = \frac{p(A, B)}{p(B)}
\]








NoteNormal data example





For a simple example, lets assume \[
D \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2),
\] where \(\mu\) is the mean, and \(\sigma^2\) is the variance of the sample.
From the measured data we are trying to infer \(\mu\) but we know \(\sigma^2\). The likelihood for this example would be, \[
p(D|\mu) = \prod_{i=1}^N \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{(D_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}} = \left(\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2 \pi}}\right)^N e^{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^N (D_i - \mu)^2},
\] where \(D_i\) is the \(i\)th data point. Therefore we have that the log-likelihood is, \[
\log \mathcal{L}(\mu) = -N(\log\sigma + \log\sqrt{2\pi}) + {-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^N (D_i - \mu)^2},
\] which has stationary points at, \[
\frac{d}{d \mu}\left\{ \log \mathcal{L}(\mu)\right\} =  {-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^N (D_i - \mu)^2} = 0.
\] The solution of which is the maximum likelihood estimate for the mean, \[
\hat{\mu} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N D_i
\]









NoteLinear Regression

















linear_regression.r

initial_samples = list(c(a = 1, b = 1, c = 0),
                       c(a = 10, b = 10, c = 10),
                       c(a = 5, b = 4, c = 1),
                       c(a = -1, b = -2, c = -3))
number_samples = 4000
proposal_sd = 2^-3

log_posterior <- function(x){
    a = x[1]
    b = x[2]
    c = x[3]
    mu = a*data$X1 + b*data$X2 + c
    return(sum(dnorm(x = data$Y, mean = mu, sd = 1, log = TRUE)))
}

transition_kernel <- function(current){
    proposed = current + rnorm(3, 0, proposal_sd)
    log_acceptance_criteria = log_posterior(proposed) + sum(dnorm(current, proposed, proposal_sd, log=TRUE)) - log_posterior(current) - sum(dnorm(proposed, current, proposal_sd, log=TRUE))
    if(log(runif(1, 0, 1)) > log_acceptance_criteria){
        proposed = current
    }
    return(proposed)
}

generate_mcmc_chain <- function(initial_sample){
    return(
           purrr::accumulate(.x = 1:number_samples,
                             .f = ~ transition_kernel(.x),
                             .init = initial_sample)
    )
}

mcmc_chains = purrr::map(.x = initial_samples,
                         .f = ~ tibble::tibble(Sample = generate_mcmc_chain(.x)) |>
                             dplyr::mutate(Iteration = dplyr::row_number())) |>
                dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "Chain") |>
                tidyr::unnest_wider(Sample) |>
                tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = c("a", "b", "c"), values_to = "Sample", names_to = "Variable")


mcmc_chains |>
    dplyr::filter(Iteration > 1000) |>
    ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = Iteration, y = Sample, color = Chain)) +
    ggplot2::geom_point() +
    ggplot2::facet_wrap(~Variable)








mcmc_chains |>
    dplyr::group_by(Variable, Chain) |>
    dplyr::arrange(Iteration, .by_group = TRUE) |>
    dplyr::mutate(Mean = slider::slide_dbl(Sample, mean, .before=499)) |>
    ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = Iteration, y = Mean, color = Chain)) +
    ggplot2::geom_point() +
    ggplot2::facet_wrap(~Variable)












Conjugate Priors
Numerical methods for sampling from complicated distributions are a relatively modern advancement. Therefore, Bayesian’s typically focused on trying to get closed-form solutions to posterior distributions. This was done through the use of Conjugate Priors.
Their use today is still important, as conjugate priors can be placed on certain parameters to improve computational efficiency.


Bayes’ Estimators
When we were investigating maximum likelihood, we obtained a point estimate for the parameters. In a similar fashion we can obtain point estimates of parameters in Bayesian Inference. These estimates minimise a loss function.
The maximum posterior estimate, whilst being an arguably obvious choice, is not always a Bayes’ estimator. Does this mean you should not use the maximum posterior as a point estimate? I am always keen for a good argument but I do not know if this one can be answered easily. You can view maximum posterior estimates as a maximum likelihood method with regularization, in which case they are valid but not Bayesian. Another criticism I would like to highlight is that the posterior distribution, in general, is not invariant undertransformation. Consider Binomial data such that the number of trials is 10 and the number of successes is 3. We have, \[
p(\theta|D) \propto \theta^3(1-\theta)^7 \theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1},
\] where we have assumed a Beta distribution prior with hyperparameters \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) and \(p\) is the probability of success. The resulting posterior (as beta distributions are conjugate to binomial distributions) is again a Beta distribution, \[
p(\theta|D) \propto \theta^{2 + \alpha}(1-\theta)^{6 + \beta},
\] which is maximised at, \[
\hat{\theta} = {\frac {1 + \alpha}{6 + \alpha +\beta}},
\] for \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta >0\). This would be our maximum posterior estimate once we decide on the value of our hyperparameters.

title: Markov Chain Monte Carlo
text:
Can you Monte Carlo your way to a Markov Chain with known stationary distribution?
Markov Chain Monte Carlo allows us to sample from the probability distribution \(\pi(x)\), which may not have been possible before.

title: Markov Chain Monte Carlo
text:
Markov Chains






NoneDiscrete Markov Chains



A discrete Markov Chain is a sequence of random variables that satisfy the Markov property. That is, the next random variable in the sequence only depends upon the current state, \[
X_{n+1} \sim P(\cdot | X_n)
\] where \(X_n\) is the \(n\)-th random variable in the sequence and \(P(\cdot | X_n)\) is the proposal distribution.








NoneDetailed Balance



\[
\pi(x)p(x'|x) = \pi(x')p(x|x')
\] where \(\pi(x)\) is the stationary distribution of the Markov Chain and \(p(x|x')\) is the transition probability from \(x'\) to \(x\). The flow out of \(x\) into \(x'\) is balanced by the flow from \(x'\) into \(x\).

title: Markov Chain Monte Carlo
text:
Markov Chain Monte Carlo
It would be extremely helpful if we could easily construct the transition probabilities of a Markov Chain with a known stationary distribution. If this was the case then we could generate a large number of samples from our Markov Chain and the stationary distribution of these samples will be samples from our distribution of interest. This is the main premise behind Markov Chain Monte Carlo, where we use a Monte Carlo approach to alter a simpler Markov Chain into one with a known stationary distribution.
To construct the transition probabilities we decompose \(p(x'|x)\) into an accept-reject step. Namely, \[
p(x'|x) = q(x'|x)A(x', x),
\] where \(q(x|x')\) is the probability density of the proposal distribution and \(A(x', x)\) is the acceptance criteria (note that it is both a function of the current state and the updated state). The accept-reject step consists of proposing a new sample, \[
x' \sim Q(\cdot|x)
\] where \(Q(\cdot|x)\) is the proposal distribution, followed by checking if we accept the new sample. We can now ask what acceptance criteria will ensure that the Markov Chain satisfies detailed balance with a stationary distribution \(\pi(x)\).






NoneMetropolis-Hastings Acceptance Criteria



\[
A(x', x) = \min \left(1, \frac{\pi(x')q(x| x')}{\pi(x)q(x' | x)}\right)
\] where \(q(x'|x)\) is probability density of the proposal distribution of \(x'\) given a known \(x\).


The Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm is a way to construct a Markov Chain with known stationary distribution. This algorithm breaks up the sampling procedure into two steps, the proposal step and the acceptance step. By using an acceptance step that satisfies detailed balance, we can ensure that the stationary distribution of the algorithm is the probability distribution we want to sample from. This is beneficial when you do not have another way to sample from the required distribution.
The full algorithm for Markov Chain Monte Carlo is:

Start with an initial sample \(x\).
Generate a proposed sample \(x' \sim Q(\cdot | x)\)
Accept sample with probability \(A(x', x)\).
Repeat steps 2-4 as desired.

This will generate a sequence of samples that have the stationary distribution \(\pi(x)\).

Example
Here we provide a simple implementation of Markov Chain Monte Carlo. Consider we want to sample from a normal distribution with mean \(40\) and standard deviation of \(2\). We can obviously sample directly from that distribution using known techniques, but lets construct a Markov Chain such that \[
\pi(x) = \mathcal{N}(x|\mu = 40, \sigma = 2).
\]



simple_mcmc.r

number_samples = 10000
initial_samples= c(1.0, 5.0, -10.0, 40.0)
mu = 40
sd = 2

transition_kernel <- function(current){
    proposed = current + rnorm(1, 0, 1)
    acceptance_criteria = dnorm(proposed, mu, sd)*dnorm(current, proposed, 1)/(dnorm(current, mu, sd)*dnorm(proposed, current, 1));
    if(runif(1, 0, 1) > acceptance_criteria){
        proposed = current
    }
    return(proposed)
}

generate_mcmc_chain <- function(initial_sample){
    return(
           purrr::accumulate(.x = 1:number_samples,
                             .f = ~ transition_kernel(.x),
                             .init = initial_sample)
    )
}

mcmc_chains = purrr::map(.x = initial_samples,
                         .f = ~ tibble::tibble(Sample = generate_mcmc_chain(.x)) |>
                             dplyr::mutate(Iteration = dplyr::row_number())) |>
                dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "Chain")

mcmc_chains |>
    ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = Iteration, y = Sample)) +
    ggplot2::geom_point() +
    ggplot2::facet_wrap(~Chain)








mcmc_chains |>
    dplyr::filter(Iteration > 250) |>
    dplyr::slice(which(Iteration %% 20 == 0)) |>
    ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = Sample)) +
    ggplot2::geom_histogram(ggplot2::aes(y = ggplot2::after_stat(density)),
                            bins = 50) +
    ggplot2::geom_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mu, sd))








There are hyperparmeters within the above algorithm that should be understood, the most important of which are associated with the proposal distribution. By calibrating the proposal distribution it is possible to end up with fast (or slower) convergence to the stationary distribution.









In our simple example the only hyperparameter within the proposal distribution is the proposal variance. Figure XX demonstrates the effect of changing the proposal variance. The time to reach the stationary distribution is obviously affected by the chosen variance and there will be an optimal choice (that is problem dependent). It is important to note that as the proposal variance increases, we also observe an increased in the auto-correlation between samples. This is partly attributed to an increased probability of the proposed sample being rejected. Having a wider proposal distribution has made it more likely that samples are rejected.






Warning



The implementation presented above is prone to numerical issues. Numerical methods in statistics often have to deal with underflow and overflow, as such it is better to do computations in log-space.








NoneProportionality



A very helpful property of the acceptance criteria is that we only need to know the stationary distribution up to a constant of proportionality. Therefore, if we have a function, \[
f(x) \propto \pi(x),
\] we can still construct the Markov Chain with stationary distribution \(\pi(x)\) by \[
A(x', x) = \min \left(1, \frac{f(x')q(x| x')}{f(x)q(x' | x)}\right).
\]


The majority of methods that speed up the convergence of Markov Chain Monte Carlo focus on choosing better proposal distributions. A small and incomplete list of these methods include:

Langevin Monte Carlo
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

title: Gibbs Sampling
text:
After learning Markov Chain Monte Carlo the obvious next question is how can I improve its performance? A natural avenue to try and improve performance is to improve how often a sample is accepted. As such, we can start to look at better proposal distributions.
To improve the choice of proposal distribution we look at the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance criteria, \[
A(x', x) = \min \left(1, \frac{\pi(x')q(x| x')}{\pi(x)q(x' | x)}\right)
\] where \(\pi(x)\) is the stationary distribution of interest and \(q(\cdot|x)\) is the proposal distribution. One choice that would improve our acceptance rate is to choose, \[
q(x|x') = \pi(x),
\] but that would suffer from the obvious problem (we built this algorithm to sample \(\pi\)…). As such, we will have to look for other alternatives.
Sometimes, definitely not always, complicated joint distributions actually have relatively simple conditional distributions. For example, if you know \[
p(A,B) = p(A|B)p(B),
\] a simple sampling algorithm consists of sampling \(B\) and then sampling \(A\) with that known value of \(B\). This has factorised the problem into two steps. With Gibbs sampling we will break up sampling from our joint distribution into sampling from conditional distributions.
The proposition behind Gibbs samplers is to take the posterior distribution and sample iteratively from each parameter. To demonstrate we assume that \(x = [x,y]\) and that we are looking at the acceptance criteria for accepting a newly proposed \(x\). In this situation, \[
A([x',y], [x,y]) = \min \left(1, \frac{\pi(x',y)q(x,y| x',y)}{p(x,y)q(x',y | x)}\right)
\] where \(\pi(x)\) is the stationary distribution of interest and \(q(\cdot|x)\) is the proposal distribution. We can expand the joint probabilities to, \[
A([x',y], [x,y]) = \min \left(1, \frac{p(x'|y)p(y)q(x,y| x',y)}{p(x|y)p(y)q(x',y | x)}\right),
\] which has the wonderful property of cancelling out \(p(y)\). So if we were to sample iteratively from our distribution we would simplify our acceptance criteria to, \[
A([x',y], [x,y]) = \min \left(1, \frac{p(x'|y)q(x,y| x',y)}{p(x|y)q(x',y | x)}\right).
\]
Given this updated form of the acceptance criteria, we can start to construct an appropriate proposal density. The more astute might notice that if we choose the proposal density as the conditional of our stationary distribution, \(q(x',y|x,y) = p(x'|y)\) then, \[
A([x',y], [x,y]) = 1,
\] and we are accepting every proposal (the same holds true for if we were proposing a new \(y\) value but we would use the conditional \(p(y|x)\) as our proposal distribution). This is exact premise behind Gibbs Sampling.
The Gibbs sampling algorithm is a Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm where each parameter is updated iteratively and the proposal distribution is the conditional distribution for that parameter. In doing this we accept every sample from our Markov Chain. There are however limitations to this technique, such as large autocorrelations, but this method has been integral to statistical methods.

title: Probability Notes
text:
I am not an expert on this fight… but here is my opinion that I have put unsolicited on the internet.
Frequentist statistics is the common first year subject at university that makes you wonder why are you checking p-values all the time. Bayesian statistics is the one you learn later on in a rush cause its cool. But what is the real difference behind them.
There is one main distinction that you should remember when talking about the difference between Bayesian and Frequentist probability. Bayesian statistics says that the parameters are random variables given the data. Frequentist statistics says that the data is a random variable given the parameters. That is, Frequentists love \[
p(D|\theta),
\] where \(D\) is the data and \(\theta\) is the parameters of interest, and Bayesians love \[
p(\theta|D).
\]
Are we done? Yes. Is there so much more to it than that super simple explanation? Yes.


Another way that makes it easier for me to think about the difference between frequentist and bayesian statistics is to think of p-values. Lets start with a simple example of the mean of a normal distribution. Let us say that we have measured 20 data points that we believe are normally distributed with an unknown mean, \(\mu\) but a known variance, \(\sigma^2\). When we think like a frequentist, we look at our data (which we believe is sampled from a distribution) and we determine an estimate for our mean. This is typically done using maximum likelihood. This is it, we are done, we have our measurement for the mean. It is, \[
\hat{\mu} = \frac{1}{10}\sum_{i=1}^20 D_i
\] where \(D_i\) is our \(i\)-th data point and \(\hat{\mu}\) is our estimate of the true mean.
But as a frequentist, we might then say… well that was our measurement but “Is it a significant measurement!”
To look at significance, we actually look at the distribution of the maximum likelihood estimate. Wait, a distribution of the maximum likelihood? That does not make sense as it is a point. Yes it is a point estimate, but what we do is we look at how that point estimate will change BECAUSE OUR DATA IS RANDOM.
The next time we collect data, we expect that we will get a different point estimate of the mean! What is the distribution? Well, \[
D_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),
\] where \(\mathcal{N}\) is used to denote the normal distribution, so we have that \[
\hat{\mu} = \frac{1}{10}\sum_{i=1}^{20} D_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{20}).
\] So because the data varies our estimate for the maximum likelihood is also a random variable! If you do not believe me, lets look at this example

estimator_data <- tibble::tibble(
  `Sample mean` = rowMeans(matrix(rnorm(n = 10000 * 20, mean = 2, sd = 1), ncol = 20))
)
ggplot2::ggplot(estimator_data, ggplot2::aes(x = `Sample mean`)) +
    ggplot2::geom_histogram(stat = "density") +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10)

Warning in ggplot2::geom_histogram(stat = "density"): Ignoring unknown
parameters: `binwidth` and `bins`









This calculates the repeated sample means that result from our varying data.
The point of p-values is to now ask the question. Given the model assumptions that we have made, what is the probability that I observed my estimated mean?
(Left as an exercise to the reader for now)
As a bayesian, we would not consider repeating the experiment over and over to determine a distribution of sample means. Instead we would use Baye’s Theorem to determine the probability distribution for the true mean. We would look at \[
p(\mu |D) \propto p(D|\mu)p(\mu),
\] where \(p(\mu|D)\) is called the posterior, \(p(D|\mu)\) is our likelihood (which is the same as the likelihood used in a frequentist version) and \(p(\mu)\) is our prior distribution. The prior distribution is of interest as it is encodes our prior belief in the value of \(\mu\) before we observed the data. If we continue with our previous example we would say that \[
p(D|\mu) = \prod_{i=1}^{20} \mathcal{N}(D_i | \mu, \sigma^2)
\] and we could say that our prior belief is that \(\mu\) is around zero. This could look like, \[
p(\mu) = \mathcal{N}(\mu|0,\lambda^2)
\] where \(\lambda\) is the variance we expect in our prior belief around \(\mu\). Having defined all of this, the distribution for our mean is, \[
p(\theta|D) \propto \prod_{i=1}^{20} \mathcal{N}(D_i | \mu, \sigma^2)\mathcal{N}(\mu|0,\lambda^2).
\]
Now that is the answer from a Bayesian perspective. We do not ask the same p-value questions as before as it does not have any meaning to us. The data that we measured updated our belief for what we think the value of \(\mu\) is.



Yeah, I hid all of the complicated nonsense hidden with a wonderful \(\propto\) sign. In doing so, I hid all of the complicated integrals and all the complicated nonsense.
So what do Bayesian people do? When it comes to evaluating their problem at the end of the day, they normally construct samplers that generate samples from their posterior distribution. Why do they use samplers? When evaluating high dimensional integrals (which that constant normally is) the monte carlo method provides wonderful convergence properties!

So what do Bayesian people do? When it comes to evaluating their problem at the end of the day, they normally construct samplers that generate samples from their posterior distribution. Why do they use samplers? When evaluating high dimensional integrals (which that constant normally is) the monte carlo method provides wonderful convergence properties!

title: Approximate Bayesian Computation
text: The new hype in model fitting is Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC). This is under development, go read.

title: Model fitting
text: When developing mathematical models you will inherently end up with parameters. These parameters may be known a-priori, for example Planck’s constant or the speed of light, but others may need to be estimated from observed data. In fact, you may have written down your model with the express intention of determining these parameters through experiment. In this section, we will work through techniques that can be used to fit models to data.

title: What if my model is not stochastic?
text: The examples provided in within this model fitting section have focused on probability distributions and determining their parameters. But what if the model you have written down is not actually a probability distribution? What if you wrote down a system of ordinary differential equations (or partial differential equations)? Are there any approaches that can be used to fit these models? Unsurprisingly yes, and the majority of which are based on maximum likelihood or Bayesian inference.

title: What if my model is not stochastic?
text:
Pitfalls of model fitting
When fitting mathematical models to data you must be able to evaluate the model relatively efficiently. There is no escaping the fact that the model must be run repeatedly to obtain information on the fit. Some models can be solved with minimal computational effort and then no real thought has to go into the best option for fitting. If you have a model that takes hours to run for a single parameter combination then you now have to think about your best approach.
